<a id="who-sets-a-confusion-seams-state"></a>

### Who sets a seam's state — the reader, or the app's guess from the data?

**open** · question · lives in [design/confusion-points.md](design/confusion-points.md#-who-sets-a-seams-state--the-reader-or-the-apps-guess-from-the-data--open)

**Where it stands (2026-10-13):** the reader owns it, and that is built: a row can be marked
Beaten or Dismissed, and nothing changes it but the reader. What is still open is only whether
the app may *suggest* a change, and how loudly.

Each confusion point carries a state — *every pass*, *sometimes*, *used to*, *dismissed* — and
the question is who writes it. The design's bet is **the reader owns it**, because the store sees
*captures*, not recitation: silence at a seam could mean *I beat it* or *I stopped logging*, and
the app cannot tell which, so a state it computed would be the very score this feature refused.
The counter-pull is friction: a reader who never taps *«beat it»* leaves conquered seams warning
forever, and a gentle inference (*nothing here in six weeks — retire it?*) would spare them. **What
would answer it:** a human's call on how strong the nudge may be — whether the app is allowed to
*suggest* a state change from `count` + recency (and how loudly), while the write itself stays an
explicit act — or whether even a suggestion leans too far toward measuring worship. Leaning
reader-owned-with-a-quiet-nudge, but the line between *nudge* and *assertion* is the thing to
settle, and it echoes the durability and score stances above.

**Owner, 2026-11-08: a quiet suggestion, yours to accept.** A row not hit in a long while may
carry one quiet line offering to mark it Beaten. Never a pop-up, and nothing changes until the
reader taps it. Not built yet; on the backlog.

<details><summary>Our notes on it</summary>

Each confusion point carries a state — every-pass, sometimes, used-to, dismissed — that drives warning weight, list grouping and map colour. The question is who writes it. The design's bet is the reader owns it, because the store sees captures, not recitation: silence at a seam could mean 'I beat it' or 'I stopped logging', and a state the app computed would be the very score this feature refused. The counter-pull is friction — a reader who never marks a seam beaten leaves conquered seams warning forever. What would answer it: a human's call on how strong the nudge may be, whether the app may suggest a state change from count + recency (and how loudly) while the write stays an explicit act, or whether even a suggestion leans too far toward measuring worship. Leaning reader-owned-with-a-quiet-nudge; the line between nudge and assertion is the thing to settle. Where it stands 2026-10-13: reader-owned is built (Beaten, Dismissed); only whether the app may suggest a change, and how loudly, is open. Owner, 2026-11-08: a quiet suggestion, the reader's to accept: one line on a row not hit in a long while, offering Beaten; never a pop-up. To build.

</details>

<a id="word-drawer-stacks-on-verse"></a>

### Should a word's drawer open on top of the verse's, so both stay in reach?

**open** · question · lives in [decisions/selection-drawer.md](decisions/selection-drawer.md#-should-a-words-drawer-open-on-top-of-the-verses-so-both-stay-in-reach--open)

**What would answer it:** a rough build where a tap on a word, with the verse drawer open, stacks
the word's drawer on top of it, tried by the owner beside today's two separate modes.

**Asked by the owner, in a comment left on the app's page (2026-11-07):** *"if I click on a word do
i get a word drawer stacked on top of it"*. Today the two never meet. With the Verse tool a tap on a
word lights its whole verse; the word's own drawer (its letters and vowel-signs) opens only with the
Word tool, and in the verse drawer's place, not above it.

**What it changes for a hafiz:** marking a slip on one vowel-sign and then listening to the verse
around it means switching tools between the two today.

**Options to build and try, each a setting if it loses:**
- the word's drawer stacks on the verse's, and closing it leaves the verse's open;
- the verse drawer gains a row of the verse's words, and a tap there opens the word below;
- the two stay separate, one per tool, as today.

**If nobody decides:** they stay separate.

**Built 2026-11-09, the first option, as a setting** (info panel, *Tapping the lit verse again*;
*Puts the verse out* stays the default until the owner has tried the other by hand). With *Opens
the word you tapped* chosen, a second tap on a word of the lit verse opens that word's letters and
signs in a drawer standing on top of the verse's drawer. The verse stays lit and its drawer stays;
Escape or a tap elsewhere closes only the word's drawer. A tap on another verse still lights that
verse, as before.

**What the rough build found, which no list had a row for:**
- The two drawers together are tall. On a laptop the word's drawer stood right over the verse it
  was about, so the page now lifts the verse clear of both, as it already does for the verse's
  drawer alone.
- The word's drawer was placed once, while the verse's drawer was still sliding in, and one time
  in thirty it overlapped it. It now follows the verse's drawer as it moves or changes size.
- It needs no new tool: it rides on the Verse tool, so marking one sign and then listening to the
  verse no longer means switching tools.

**Left:** the owner tries the setting on the laptop and the iPad and says whether it becomes the
default. The second option (a row of the verse's words in the drawer) is not built.

<details><summary>Our notes on it</summary>

Owner's page comment of 2026-11-07 asked whether a tap on a word opens a word drawer stacked on the verse drawer. Today the Verse tool lights the verse and only the Word tool opens the word's drawer, in the same place. Built 2026-11-09 as a setting in the info panel (putting the verse out stays the default): a second tap on a word of the lit verse opens its letters and signs in a drawer on top of the verse's, both stay, and the page lifts the verse clear of the two. Left: the owner tries the setting and says whether it becomes the default. Checked 2026-11-10: going full screen or picking another tool is a tap outside the word's drawer, which closes it, and the keys for both do nothing while it is open. Moving to another verse or page by the address (the back button, a link from another app) left it floating over the next verse; fixed the same day, so it closes when its verse's drawer moves on (browser tests in the word-stack tests).

</details>

<a id="plan-loop-assigned-deferrals"></a>

### Loop-assigned deferrals

**blocked** · question · waiting on loop-7 · lives in [PLAN.md](PLAN.md#open-follow-ups)

Loop-assigned deferrals (already scoped in their loop sections; details in the decision
records): full corpus vendoring + QUL validation → **done, Loop 4b**;
**word-granularity roots + `?w=` UI** and **word-granularity tajweed painting** — both
said "after 4b", and 4b's answer is that the shipped corpus has no word geometry at all,
so they move behind **follow-up 13** rather than behind a loop (the tajweed spans are
still vendored verbatim, so that one stays a rendering change once geometry exists).
13 is answered as of 2026-08-04 — the candidate corpus is our print — so what stands
between here and both features is no longer a corpus hunt but registering its word boxes
onto our page frame and vendoring the result;
**and as of 2026-08-06 that registration is two loops behind us and this entry had not
noticed.** The boxes shipped (word-B) and so did the alignment (word-D), so
**word-granularity roots + `?w=` UI is done** — the param is documented in
[`query-params.md`](query-params.md) and the run announces its own outcome. Word-granular
**tajweed** painting is the half that is left, and its wall is not the one written above:
the annotations are codepoint offsets into a Tanzil Uthmani text this repo does not hold
and will not. That is its own row — [`word-indexing.md` ⑤](design/word-indexing.md) —
because a deferral re-pointed four times is a register asking to be split, and the split
is what made the remaining work visible instead of merely deferred. **⑤ is answered the
same day it was split, and it answered against its own prediction:** it expected a third
segmentation and got a build change. `pnpm probe:tajweed-words` reconstructs the Tanzil
string from the print's own per-word `data-hafs` — nothing vendored, the no-text rule
intact — under eight corrections: three **structural** ones the corpus states rather than
guesses (basmala prefix, the print's split conjunction waw which it flags itself, pause
marks the print numbers as words) and five **orthographic** ones found by bracketing each
failing ayah between its last correct annotation and its first wrong one — a tatweel
carrying a small high mark, «أٓ», the small high madda, the hamza below, and the sakta
seen where it ends a word. It lands **99.86%** of a character oracle on the exact expected
letter — over **all 60,057 annotations**, since every one of the source's eighteen rules
now names its letters, and **93.65%** of that once each check is weighted by the chance it
could have failed — with **83.31%** of annotations inside one print word and **16.69%**
across two adjacent ones — the cross-word phonology, paintable as a range. What is left is
an ordinary bake with a **ten-ayah exception list, every entry named** (three of them names
the repo already carries in `lib/segmentation.mjs`), not a corpus hunt. `pnpm
probe:encodings` ([encoding-inspector.md](design/encoding-inspector.md)) is the instrument
those corrections were read off, and where a ninth would be. The beta label is unaffected
either way, because it hangs on the palette, not the geometry; **hafiz
sign-off on the tajweed skin → Loop 7** (the beta label stays until then). **Done:**
golden-image visual regression, Lighthouse CI, and the **⬡ chip vs ⬡ lens** collision —
all Loop 6a ([loop-6a.md](decisions/loop-6a.md)); marquee drag-select (Loop 5);
per-polygon a11y labels + keyboard hop path (Loop 3); `navigateTo` animation (Loop 2).

The word-granular items said 'after 4b' and 4b's answer is that the adopted corpus has no word geometry at all, so they now wait on plan-word-geometry-is-a-second-corpus rather than on a loop. The hafiz sign-off on the tajweed skin waits on loop-7. Re-pointed rather than closed: the blockers moved, the item did not. Still blocked on 2026-08-04, and worth being precise about why: plan-word-geometry-is-a-second-corpus is now answered, but what it answered is the print question — the candidate corpus is our V2 — not the geometry question. Its own probe found the next wall (a different viewBox and page frame, so no word box transfers without per-page registration), so these deferrals wait on that work, which follow-up 13 now names and task #65 carries. <a id="plan-qul-harakat"></a>

### Can the library's page pick out a single harakah, and should it?

**blocked** · question · waiting on bringing the app's own per-mark ink geometry (already shipped on the mark-work branch) onto this feature's branch, then giving the existing mistake-marking a single-mark anchor — a product step plus a branch-convergence the owner steers · lives in [PLAN.md](PLAN.md#open-follow-ups)

**Can the library's page pick out a single harakah, and should it?** Asked 2026-09-08. The
 short answer is no, not as the page is drawn today, and the longer answer is a question for
 the owner rather than a build.
 **Why not today:** the per-page font draws each printed word as *one* character with its
 vowel and reading marks already part of the shape. There is no separate character for a
 fatha or a shadda to select, hide or colour; the tajweed colouring in the library's cut is
 baked into each word's shape by the font itself.
 **What it would take:** the library's plain Unicode word text (where a word is letters plus
 combining marks, each mark its own character) and its single Unicode Hafs face (resource
 245), neither of which is held. With those, marks can be filtered by kind at the text level —
 show or hide every sukun, every shadda — cheaply; colouring one mark on its own in a browser
 is not cheap, because a browser will not style half a shaped word, so it means drawing the
 text ourselves. Both files are Qur'an text and would join the held copy under the same
 licence read and the same never-in-the-tree rule.
 **What is open:** what the owner wants a selectable harakah *for* — a reading check, a
 tajweed lesson, a comparison against the print's own marks — decides whether the cheap
 filter is enough or the expensive drawing is needed, and whether either earns holding two
 more files. Nothing is fetched until that is said. Blocks nothing shipped.

<details><summary>Our notes on it</summary>

CORRECTED 2026-09-09 after checking the mark-work branch directly. The earlier note here said the per-mark geometry was 'not yet shipped as an asset' and told a reader not to touch the 'sibling branch'. Both are wrong. There is one operator, not two; and the geometry IS shipped: the app's own ink-derived per-mark rectangles ride as a static asset, one file per page for all 604 pages, each mark carrying its word, its name (kasra, sukun, fatha, shadda, wasla, superscript alef and the rest), a rectangle, and whether it was placed on its own ink or by hand. That is exactly the granularity a single harakah needs, and it settles the feasibility this row asks about: per-harakah marking is reachable on our OWN print, with NO held Qur'an text and NO outside font — so this row's title, which assumed the library's Unicode word text and Unicode Hafs face were required, had the wrong route. That is route 1, and the placement is already decided (option H) and corrected (the marks sit on their ink, not on the raw displaced rectangles the mark-placement finding measured). Owner intent, unchanged: reader interaction at one mark — a hafiz pinning a personal recitation slip finer than a word, and flagging where the printed mus'haf or our drawing of it is off at one mark. What is genuinely left is a product step, not data: extend the existing mistake-marking so its anchor can be a single mark, and bring the shipped geometry and this feature onto one branch to do it. The only still-open refinement is the per-line bend correction (a finer, line-by-line tilt on top of the per-mark placement), which waits on the owner's own eye before it ships — polish, not a blocker for a first per-harakah anchor. Related: mistake-marking, mark-granularity, mark-registration. Fetch nothing held.

</details>

<a id="sharing-sign-in"></a>

### If accounts come, which ways of signing in, and do they work inside the iPad and Mac apps?

**blocked** · question · waiting on sharing-which-way · lives in [design/sharing-between-readers.md](design/sharing-between-readers.md#-if-accounts-come-which-ways-of-signing-in-and-do-they-work-inside-the-ipad-and-mac-apps--blocked)

Asked by both. Suggested: Sign in with Apple and an email link, tried on a throwaway test project in both apps; Google later through the system browser; passkeys once Supabase's support settles. **What would answer it:** waits on the choice of way (③); the live locked link needs no sign-in.

**What we know so far about Sign in with Apple (2026-11-11, from the hifth.app plan).** Nothing built; written down so the decision starts from it.

- **Nothing needs an account today.** Your own iPad and Mac keep in step through your own iCloud; a teacher's copy is a file first and a link with no account next; the notify-me list needs none. So the front page has no "Sign in" button: a button with nothing behind it promises what the page cannot keep.
- **Where it would live:** `hifth.app`, the address Hifth owns (⑧, ⑭). Apple ties a sign-in to the name it was set up on, so this matters once and is now settled.
- **In the iPad and Mac apps:** Apple's own sign-in sheet, its answer handed to the page through the bridge the apps already have. No sign-in web pages inside the app's built-in browser.
- **In a browser:** Apple's web sign-in for hifth.app. Apple sends its answer back by posting a form to a return address, so there has to be a small server part to receive it: a function on the same Cloudflare account as the notify list, or Supabase's ready-made one.
- **Which server.** Cloudflare's functions and small database sit beside the notify list and never pause. Supabase's sign-in is ready-made, but its free plan pauses a project after a week unused, and it would have to be a new project, never the one holding the outside library.
- **Apple's rules that come with it.** An app that makes accounts must let you delete yours inside the app. If Google sign-in is ever offered, Sign in with Apple must be too. Apple sends the name and email only the first time someone signs in, so they must be kept then.
- **What would answer it, once ③ says accounts:** a throwaway trial in both apps on a test sign-in setup for hifth.app. That waits on the apps being signed with the paid Apple team.

<details><summary>Our notes on it</summary>

If accounts come: try Sign in with Apple and an email link inside the iPad and Mac apps on a throwaway test project; Google later through the system browser. The live locked link needs no sign-in. 2026-11-11: what is known about Sign in with Apple is written into ⑨ (where it lives, the server it needs, Apple's rules, the trial); still blocked on ③.

</details>

<a id="testflight-sign-with-paid-team"></a>

### Sign the app with the paid team and reinstall it on the owner's iPad and Mac

**blocked** · question · waiting on the Mac install is still to do · lives in [design/testflight-plan.md](design/testflight-plan.md#-sign-the-app-with-the-paid-team-and-reinstall-it-on-the-owners-ipad-and-mac--blocked)

The agent's, now that the team ID is known (①). Installs then last a year instead of seven days.

**The iPad is done (2026-11-10).** The paid team signed it, the install has 364 days left, and
it goes on with `make app-release-ipad DEVICE=…`, which runs the verse-touch test on the iPad's
own OS first and fails on a new crash report after. Its first install closed on a touch; that
was fixed the same day (`docs/issues/ipad-crash-on-verse-touch.md`). **Left: the Mac.**

**Next for the pitch: walk the six passages on the real iPad.** Every walk so far ran in the
simulator, and the simulator missed the touch crash. Unlock the iPad and leave it plugged in. Xcode is signed in since 2026-11-09, and
its Accounts screen shows the paid Developer Team. (The first try that day stopped because no
account was signed in; the install command now checks for one first.)

**How the install proves the year.** After the build, the install command reads the signing
profile inside the app and counts the days it has left. A year means the paid team signed it and
the install goes on. A few days means a free team did, and it stops before anything reaches the
iPad. It also stops if Xcode reused an old profile with under a month left, so the app cannot run
out the week of the meeting. Xcode's own saved settings are not trusted for this: that day they
still said "Personal Team" while the Accounts screen showed the paid team.

**No cable needed after the first time, and nothing uploaded.** Xcode installs over Wi-Fi when the
laptop and the device share a network. On iOS or iPadOS 27 and later it pairs with no cable at
all; on older versions, one cable pairing first. TestFlight would also install without a cable,
but it uploads the build to Apple, which the licence decision does not allow yet
([research note](research/2026-11-09-testflight-own-devices.md); the licence brief now asks
about that narrower step as question 6).

<details><summary>Our notes on it</summary>

2026-11-10: the iPad is done. The paid team signed it (364 days left) and `make app-release-ipad` puts it on with the verse-touch test first and a crash-report check after; the touch crash its first install showed is fixed (docs/issues/ipad-crash-on-verse-touch.md). Next for the pitch: walk the six passages on the real iPad, since the simulator missed that crash. Left on this row: the Mac. Earlier (2026-11-09): the demo passes in the iPad simulator but is not on a real iPad yet. Xcode is signed in and shows the paid Developer Team. Once the iPad is plugged in, run the install; it reads the signing profile inside the built app and goes on only when it has 30 or more days left (a year from the paid team), so a free team's 7-day install or an old reused profile stops before reaching the iPad. Then the Mac.

</details>
